top.title: Warriors star Steph Curry claps back at weird podcast criticism of wife Ayesha Curry
top.description: Golden State Warriors guard Stephen Curry looks on during warmups ahead of a game on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in San Francisco. (Heather Diehl/Associated Press) HOUSTON - Stephen Curry was evidently none too pleased with social-media chatter around wife Ayesha Curry's first feature-film leading role in the romantic comedy "Second Chance Holiday." A clip from the film, featuring Ayesha Curry giving an on-screen kiss to co-star Matthew Daddario, went viral this past week and served as fodder for a wide variety of podcasts. Former NBA All-Star Gilbert Arenas and former Golden State Warriors backup Nick Young held a 17-minute segment Saturday on the kiss, with Arenas saying "the only blemish in the (Curry) family is the wife." Media personality Emmanuel Acho also devoted a good bit of airtime to the topic. On Wednesday, Curry took to Instagram for a notably pointed response. "I've been hearing a lot of noise, and usually the noise doesn't bother me, doesn't bother Ayesha, but this one in particular - when you're trying to step on the accomplishments of my wife, and obviously needing podcast tapings and topics and giving opinions on somebody else's wife - Nick, (Gilbert), Emmanuel, and anybody else who feels the need to want to have to jump in and give an opinion on something you don't really know about and kinda speaks to a bigger conversation on how you view women in this world and what they're allowed and what they're not allowed to do, even the ignorance behind how acting works," Curry said, cycling through an array of mocking faces. "Obviously, I tried to laugh this one off," he continued. "But something needs to be said. And anytime Ayesha Curry shows up in your headline, I kindly suggest you just give the happy hands, the congratulations, and maybe, just maybe, the apology can be as loud as y'all leading y'all shows with this topic." The video was clearly filmed handheld, at the spur of the moment. A source with direct knowledge of Curry's thinking said that the video response wasn't planned or organized by his team in any way, and came directly from Curry. The majority of Arenas and Young's content centered on the odd idea of Ayesha Curry potentially bringing a negative perception to the Curry family due to her acting career, visibility and independent personal success, a narrative that has existed on social media for years as her husband has simultaneously become one of the most famous athletes on the planet. Curry has increasingly dipped into the Hollywood space in recent years, starring in the animated film "GOAT" and directing the short documentary "The Baddest Speechwriter of All" this year. Back on the court, Curry has led the Warriors to an 8-3 start in 2026-27, averaging 30.6 points, 4.1 rebounds and 4.3 assists in one of the hottest early-season stretches of his career. top.title: Princeton's Kam Mercer officially signs with UC Bearcats basketball
top.description: Almost six months after his commitment was shown on ESPN's SportsCenter , Princeton High School senior Kameron "Kam" Mercer returned to the same room to officially sign with the Cincinnati Bearcats on Nov. 11. It was no surprise, as Mercer has been at UC games and was one of new coach Jerrod Calhoun's priorities when he arrived in town in late March. Mercer helped the Vikings win the Ohio Division I state title on March 22, then Calhoun was introduced as UC's head coach the following day. Mercer had been offered by previous coach Wes Miller's staff in eighth grade. Not long after his introductory press conference, Calhoun was on the phone with Princeton coach Bryan Wyant, asking if his staff had a chance with Mercer. The sales pitch succeeded and Mercer has been "all-in" on UC and Calhoun. After UC's difficult 63-61 loss to Minnesota, Mercer posted on X: "In him I trust" with a picture of himself with Calhoun. During his signing ceremony, he became emotional while talking about his parents, Craig and Nicole Mercer. His mother came to the podium to comfort her 6-foot-5 son. "I believe so much in Calhoun and what he's done," Mercer said. "I know he took a tough loss to Minnesota. I'm not really worried about one game. I'm super excited to get to the next level and play for him. I'm a guy that's going to come in on Day One and be a leader. Somebody that wants to win. I want to become a winner I want to become an NCAA champion." In him I trust🫡. https://t.co/jzYQJqQ4oX — Kameron Mercer (@kameron_mercer) November 10, 2026 Mercer led the Princeton Vikings to a state crown as a sophomore, averaging 14.2 points and 5.4 rebounds per game with 3.4 assists and 2.4 steals per contest. Playing at Huntington Expression Prep in West Virginia as a freshman against older talent, he averaged 11 points, 6 rebounds and 5 assists. He moved up a year scholastically to join the Bearcats for 2027-28. He also attended future teammate Josh Tyson's commitment to UC in September . Tyson played against Mercer at Lakota West but is now playing at La Lumiere in Indiana. Princeton coach Bryan Wyant has been at numerous UC basketball practices and has incorporated some of their strategies into his Vikings. Wyant believes doing so will give Mercer an advantage as a freshman Bearcat. For now, Wyant is very bullish on Mercer. "I think he has a chance to be one of the most dominant players that we've seen in the last 20 years," he said. "I've only been here 20 years, so that's all I can speak for. I'm talking about actual production on the floor. If he can keep progressing, I think he can have a chance at one of the special seasons that we've seen over the last 20 years." The Cougars checked in at No. 14 in the latest CFP rankings released Tuesday, a three-spot jump from the previous week. If the playoff began today, the Cougars would miss the cut in the current 12-team format. Under the expanded format for next season - which will include the four champions from the Power Four conferences (SEC, Big 12, Big Ten and ACC), the highest-ranked Group of Six champion and 19 at-large selections - the Cougars would be in position to host a first-round playoff game. To have any chance in this era of college football, you must have an invitation. Otherwise, you can spend your holiday at the Alamo Bowl or Pop-Tarts Bowl. Nothing wrong with those postseason destinations, but the ceiling has been raised for a UH program that is now among the top 15 in the nation. It's been a hard climb. The last time the Cougars were in the national discussion was during the H-Town Takeover, a two-year window that included wins over behemoths Florida State, Oklahoma and Louisville. top.title: MSCI Removes Strategy (MSTR) From Its USA Index, Forcing Index Funds to Sell by Nov. 30
top.description: Bitcoin Magazine MSCI Removes Strategy (MSTR) From Its USA Index, Forcing Index Funds to Sell by Nov. 30 MSCI will remove Strategy, the largest corporate bitcoin holder, from the MSCI USA Index as of the close of Nov. 30, the index provider said Wednesday, after a new screen classified the company as a non-operating issuer. The decision is part of MSCI’s November 2026 Index Review , posted shortly after 5 p.m. ET. Official additions and deletions lists show Strategy (MSTR) out of its USA Index, which also takes it out of the broader MSCI World and ACWI indexes. The same review deletes Japan’s Metaplanet from the MSCI Japan Small Cap Index and uranium holder Yellow Cake from the MSCI United Kingdom Small Cap Index, and it removes Iceland’s Skel Fjárfestingafélag from the MSCI Iceland Frontier Markets Small Cap Index and micro-cap Upexi from the USA Micro Cap Index. All five had already been marked Deleted on MSCI’s potential-impact list , built on Sept. 30 financial data and Oct. 9 market values. Strategy is the only large-cap name in the group and, on that October list, accounted for more than 90% of the five companies’ combined float-adjusted market value. The company held 850,364 bitcoin as of Nov. 8, acquired at an average price of $75,456 a coin, or $64.16 billion in aggregate. Strategy shares closed at $122.35, up 1.06%, then slipped 1.51% to $120.50 in after-hours trading as of 5:34 p.m. ET. How the MSCI screen works The rule does not mention bitcoin. The index first checks whether a company’s operating assets equal at least 50% of total assets. Issuers that fail that core screen face five financial ratios, and a company flagged on four or more of them is ineligible for the MSCI Global Investable Market Indexes. Buffers limit turnover. A company outside the indexes cannot be added if it fails the ineligibility screen in either of its two most recent annual filing periods, but a current constituent is removed only if it fails in each of them. The index said it may also use the most recent interim filing. MSCI also said Wednesday that the same non-operating treatment will apply to the MSCI US Index Series. The screen replaces an approach aimed squarely at crypto. The index first proposed in late 2025 to exclude companies whose digital assets made up 50% or more of total assets, then dropped that plan in January and opened a broader consultation in August. It adopted the new methodology on Oct. 15, with minor modifications, and said it would end the interim measures it had placed on those companies in October 2025, including a freeze on share-count increases and a deferral of additions. What the deletion does and does not do Funds that track an MSCI index have to hold what the index holds, so they will have to sell the deleted stocks by the Nov. 30 close. Other than the Dodgers’ National League Championship Series exit, the three-month fling was as happy of a partnership as either side could have hoped. Skubal jelled with the group immediately, becoming especially close friends with fellow lefty Blake Snell, who promised that he’d worked to recruit Skubal back this offseason. And after posting a 2.61 ERA in 10 starts , Skubal, the Dodgers’ Game 1 starter in both playoff series, limited postseason opponents to a total of three runs. “I know that he enjoyed his time here, we loved having him, so I think that’s certainly helpful as far as these conversations go,” Dodgers general manager Brandon Gomes said Tuesday at General Managers meetings. “And outside of that, he’s earned the right to be in this position and figure out what’s best for him and his family.” That position, while it guarantees him a highly lucrative contract, is complicated by the impending lockout. Skubal’s agent, Scott Boras , when asked during his media availability Wednesday whether he’d consider a shorter deal with a higher average annual value, said he wouldn’t discuss contract negotiations. But creativity around the structure of a deal could help counter teams’ anxieties over a possible salary cap in the next Collective Bargaining Agreement. top.title: What Reggie Gilliam’s return designation means for the Patriots
top.description: For the first time in five weeks, the New England Patriots had a traditional fullback at practice on Wednesday. Reggie Gilliam, who was initially placed on injured reserve due to knee and ankle injuries in early October, made his comeback during his team’s final session before its trip to Germany for the upcoming Week 10 meeting with the Detroit Lions. This means he is now officially designated to return from IR. Let’s check out how this impacts the Patriots for the time being. Clock starts ticking We will get into the actual on-field impact of a potential Gilliam return to the 53-man roster once/if he is activated. For now, at least, the window for such a follow-up move has been opened. This means that, at least theoretically, Gilliam could be back on the game day roster as soon as this Sunday against the Lions. He will join the rest of the team on the flight to Germany, so there is an option New England could activate him in time for the game. They don’t have to, however: the team has 21 days to make that call before the return window will close again. If not activated at that point, Gilliam would revert back to injured reserve to end his season. Obviously, with return designations limited — more on that in a second — the expectation is is that the 29-year-old will eventually return to the 53-man roster when all is said and done. Two guys, one spot Following Monday’s release of tight end Tanner Arkin — a move that might hint at a potential Gilliam activation given that the rookie served as a stand-in fullback over the last few weeks — the Patriots have 52 of the 53 spots on their active roster occupied. This means that they could easily activate Gilliam without having to make a follow-up move. There is only one problem: he is not the only player currently in the 21-day window. Interior offensive lineman Greg Van Roten, who was the next man up after starting right guard Mike Onwenu fractured his ankle in September, returned to practice last week. He too is a candidate to be activated, especially given the current state of New England’s interior offensive line. top.title: Tennessee basketball’s mock CBA offers glimpse into college sports’ future
top.description: Tennessee guard Dai Dai Ames (4) shoots between Radford guard Tristan Gross (10) and guard Jordyn Kee (3) during the second half of an NCAA college basketball game, Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026, in Knoxville, Tenn. | Wade Payne College athletics has spent the past several years trying to figure out how to operate like a professional sports business without actually becoming one. Players are getting paid. Schools are navigating revenue-sharing agreements. Athletic departments are searching for new revenue streams. And lawmakers are attempting to regulate an ever-changing industry. Now, the University of Tennessee men’s basketball team is offering another possible piece of the puzzle. Tennessee players, working with Athletes.org, released a proposed collective bargaining term sheet Tuesday after months of discussions with the school’s athletic department. The exercise wasn’t intended to create a binding agreement. Instead, it was designed to show what a formal relationship between college athletes and their schools could look like. The men’s team elected Tyler Lundblade, Campbell Duncan and DeWayne Brown II to work with the college players’ union on the proposal. Negotiations stretched across August and September before both sides finalized terms on October 1. The proposal could offer a glimpse into where college athletics is headed, particularly as Congress considers new legislation and schools like Utah continue exploring different financial models. It addresses everything from player compensation and health care to transfer rules and offseason commitments. Among its more notable provisions are a salary cap and spending floor, guaranteed compensation for injured players, postseason bonuses, additional medical coverage and mutually agreed-upon transfer portal rules. It would also replace the current patchwork of revenue-sharing payments and university-affiliated NIL deals with a universal athletic services agreement that compensates athletes for playing their sports rather than completing promotional obligations. In other words, it attempts to create something college athletics has largely avoided: a more structured system in which players have a direct voice in determining the rules. The proposal isn’t a signed agreement, and Tennessee’s administration hasn’t ratified the terms. nigeria.title: Spain coach optimistic over Yamal’s fitness for England Nations League clash
nigeria.description: Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said Wednesday he is optimistic Barcelona winger Lamine Yamal will be fit to face England in the Nations League at the weekend. The 19-year-old winger will miss the world champions’ visit to face the Czech Republic in Prague on Thursday with a knee problem and is set to join up with Spain after that game. Yamal played for Barcelona in the 2-1 La Liga win over Atletico Madrid on Sunday and on Monday Spain said he would not travel to face the Czechs. “He got hurt in the last match, he had some discomfort in one knee, he went for the usual treatment, a scan in Barcelona, and they saw he had inflammation and fluid in the knee — that meant he needed rest,” De la Fuente told reporters. “Our medical staff and his medical staff have a fantastic relationship, and I decided that his trip here should be avoided without knowing whether he’d be in any condition to play.” The coach said he had spoken to the winger and his recovery was looking positive ahead of England’s visit to Madrid on Sunday. “He’s doing a series of exercises with his physio and with the club that indicate the recovery is going well,” continued De la Fuente. “We believe, I’m optimistic, that on Friday he’ll be with us.” De la Fuente dismissed the idea that Yamal, who came third in the Ballon d’Or voting in October, has any special privileges compared to his La Roja team-mates. “He has no privileges, and his team-mates are relaxed about it, because we treat everyone the same,” added the coach. “In similar situations we would have done exactly the same for any other player, and the players know that.” – Unstoppable run – Spain have won all four games so far in Group A3 and sealed qualification to the quarter-finals. De la Fuente’s side are unbeaten in their last 43 competitive outings, and the coach said it provided his team with extra motivation. “We want to keep setting new milestones, and this is another one,” explained De la Fuente. “None of us would probably ever have thought we’d even reach 35, because we already felt those were astronomical numbers, but having reached 43, you think, my goodness, we want to get to 44, of course we do.” Spain won their previous outing away in Croatia with a brace from Arsenal’s Mikel Merino. The midfielder is frequently used as a substitute by De la Fuente to great effect, with Merino netting vital goals against Portugal and Belgium in the World Cup off the bench this summer. Merino said he would like to be a starter for Spain but he would not kick up a fuss. “Of course, what player wouldn’t like to get (more) minutes?” Merino told reporters. “You’ll never hear me complain about the coach’s decision, I will respect it… but all players want to be important, have minutes and enjoy themselves on the pitch.” The post Spain coach optimistic over Yamal’s fitness for England Nations League clash appeared first on Vanguard News .

nigeria.description: The Canada government has announced plans to accelerate permanent residence (PR) processing for up to 200,000 foreign nationals already living in the country in 2027, as part of efforts to reduce immigration application backlogs and provide greater certainty for newcomers. The initiative, announced by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) under the 2027–2029 Immigration Levels Plan, will provide additional admissions spaces for selected workers and humanitarian applicants seeking to transition to permanent residence. According to the government, the measure will be implemented through two major groups: a workers’ cohort and a humanitarian cohort, with up to 100,000 spaces allocated to each. The workers’ category will cover eligible foreign workers already living in Canada, alongside their accompanying family members. The government intends to work with provincial and territorial authorities to identify workers who meet regional labour market requirements. Eligible workers will include those who qualify for permanent residence through the Provincial Nominee Program (PNP), as well as applicants awaiting decisions under selected federal immigration programmes. These programmes include the Atlantic Immigration Program, Start-Up Visa Program, Self-Employed Persons Program, Agri-Food Pilot and Home Care Worker programmes. The humanitarian category, also allocated up to 100,000 spaces, will cover people already in Canada who have been waiting for permanent residence decisions, including applicants under specific family reunification and humanitarian pathways. Among those expected to benefit from the humanitarian allocation are: Spouses, common-law partners and dependent children: Family members of Canadian citizens and permanent residents who have already applied for permanent residence and are awaiting final decisions. Hong Kong residents: Applicants under Canada’s permanent residence pathways for Hong Kong residents, which closed to new applications on August 31, 2026. Ukrainian nationals: Applicants under the Ukraine Family Reunification Pathway, which closed to new applications on October 22, 2024. Humanitarian and compassionate applicants: Individuals already in Canada whose applications for permanent residence have received approval in principle. The government said the additional spaces would help it process all remaining applications under the Hong Kong and Ukraine pathways, while also supporting family reunification and fulfilling existing humanitarian commitments. IRCC also said the initiative would help reduce waiting periods for spouses and partners of Canadian citizens and permanent residents, with the aim of bringing processing times closer to 12 months for applicants destined for provinces outside Quebec. nigeria.description: The United States has withdrawn from the upcoming Under-17 soccer World Cup in Qatar due to concerns about security in the Middle East, US media reported Wednesday. Players were informed of the decision just over a week before the tournament is due to begin on November 19, US Soccer Collective and The Athletic reported, citing anonymous sources. US Soccer, the sport’s governing body in the United States, did not immediately confirm the news or respond to AFP’s request for comment. The war in the Middle East began in February with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which retaliated by targeting, among others, Gulf countries allied with Washington. Diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have been punctuated by repeated threats from the United States and Israel to resume bombardments of Iran. Multiple sporting events in the Middle East have been affected, including the tennis WTA Finals which were scheduled to be held in Saudi Arabia — which neighbors Qatar — but are instead now taking place at Indian Wells in the US. This season’s Formula One Grand Prix in Jeddah was cancelled, while the race in Bahrain was called off and later rescheduled under the same name in Malaysia. Several events in Saudi Arabia have also been cancelled or postponed in recent weeks following attacks on the country by the Houthis in Yemen. The US is one of 48 teams scheduled to play in the Under-17 World Cup, in a group with Montenegro, Chile and Algeria. The Under-17 World Cup shifted to an annual event last year, and is being held in Qatar for five consecutive years. Announcing its host decision in 2024, FIFA said the decision to choose a single host nation for multiple editions centered on the ability to make “use of existing footballing infrastructure in the interest of tournament efficiencies and sustainability”. nigeria.title: Five factors vehicle buyers should consider – Understanding the true cost of ownership in Nigeria
nigeria.description: By Theodore opara Buying a vehicle is a major financial decision, but many Nigerian motorists focus almost entirely on the amount required to acquire one. While the purchase price is an important consideration, it does not tell the complete story of what it takes to own and maintain a vehicle over the years. From routine servicing and parts replacement, to insurance, fuel and unexpected repairs, vehicle ownership comes with recurring expenses that can significantly influence its overall value. For individuals, families and businesses, understanding these costs before making a purchase can help prevent financial surprises and support better decisions. The ownership cost equation Two vehicles with similar showroom prices may have significantly different maintenance requirements and operating costs. One may benefit from an established after-sales network, readily available spare parts and predictable servicing expenses. Another may present challenges when replacement components are required or technical support is unavailable. These differences can influence the overall cost of ownership. For instance, a vehicle that requires expensive repairs or spends considerable time in a workshop may eventually cost its owner more than initially anticipated. For businesses operating fleets, the consequences can be even greater. Every day a vehicle remains unavailable could affect deliveries, customer service, employee movement and revenue generation. Consequently, vehicle buyers should consider not only acquisition costs but also the financial implications of keeping their vehicles operational. Five factors buyers should consider A proper assessment of vehicle ownership costs should include five major areas. First is the purchase price and any associated financing charges. Second is routine maintenance, including scheduled servicing, lubricants, filters, tyres and other consumables. Third is warranty protection, particularly its duration, coverage and exclusions. Fourth is the availability and cost of replacement parts, including access to qualified technicians. Fifth is downtime, which may create additional transportation expenses, lost business opportunities and reduced productivity. Although some expenses are difficult to forecast, obtaining reliable information before purchasing can help buyers make more informed comparisons. They also need dependable support throughout the ownership period. nigeria.title: Uganda ruling party rejects plan for son to succeed president
nigeria.description: The leadership of Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni’s party has rejected his plan to designate his son, known for boasting of kidnapping and torturing rivals, as his successor, five party sources told AFP on Wednesday. The president’s son, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, 52, is currently head of the army, and wields huge and growing influence as his 82-year-old father plays a declining role in governing the east African country after four decades in power. “Muhoozi”, as he is widely known, has vowed to run in the next presidential election scheduled for 2031, but many are unnerved by his flouting of the law, and inflammatory posts on social media, where he frequently boasts of torturing opponents in his “basement”. In recent months, he has had political rivals imprisoned, threatened to behead opposition leader Bobi Wine, and forced the closure of the country’s leading independent media group for several weeks. Although Museveni has ruled with an iron grip since 1986, many within his party, the National Resistance Movement (NRM), have voiced concern at the apparent moves to hand power to his son. In a closed-door meeting of the NRM’s executive committee on Tuesday, convened to determine a successor, a vote on the son’s candidacy had to be abandoned as several of the 28 members spoke against the plan and received loud cheers, according to five people present. Four people had voted in favour of the son, three had voted against, by the time the vote was called off, the sources told AFP. “The combative nature of the (army chief) has created uneasiness among some people. He is fighting and threatening people on social media. Let him start convincing people but not using coercive means to capitulate the population,” said one source. NRM vice-chairman Calvin Echodu told Museveni to retire the son from the army and give him a civilian assignment to get acquainted with the population and prepare himself well for leadership,” said another participant. Echodu also reportedly advised the president that he should stand again in 2031 “as his son is not yet ready,” the source added. The attendees say it was an unprecedented show of defiance against the long-ruling president, who first broached the subject of his succession by presenting a paper to the party grandees in late October, in which he suggested his son had the right credentials for the job. The call was made at the 2026 Annual General Meeting (AGM) and Scientific Conference of the Medical Women’s Association of Nigeria (MWAN), Lagos State Branch, where the keynote speaker, Professor Kikelomo Ololade Wright, challenged female doctors to move beyond clinical practice and take their rightful place in healthcare policy formulation and strategic decision-making. According to her, United Nations figures showed that approximately 75,000 Nigerian women died from pregnancy and childbirth-related complications in 2023, representing nearly three in every 10 maternal deaths recorded globally. “That is one woman every seven minutes,” she said, describing the situation as alarming, particularly because many of the deaths were preventable. Wright, a Professor of Public Health and Community Medicine at the Lagos State University College of Medicine, insisted that women physicians must not limit their contributions to treating patients but should also influence the policies and decisions that determine healthcare delivery. “Not on the sidelines, not behind, not supporting, but we’re at the front,” she declared, stressing that women doctors must be represented in hospital boards, health committees and other decision-making platforms. “We deliver most of the care. We must also shape the decisions. It is non-negotiable,” she added. She said Nigeria’s maternal mortality ratio of estimated 993 deaths per 100,000 live births was about five times the global average and significantly higher than the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) target of 70 deaths per 100,000 live births. nigeria.description: An art project that started as a final-year assessment at Auchi Polytechnic, Auchi, Edo State, Nigeria, has turned into a full-time career for Konboye Eugene. In his studio in Kuto, Abeokuta, Ogun State, the Nigerian artist is giving discarded footwear a new lease of life, transforming them into colourful portraits. “I’ve been a full-time studio practitioner for about seven years now. I started when I was in my final year at Auchi Polytechnic, where I studied painting,” Eugene said. “It started as an assignment for me when I was in school. But over the course of my practice, I have become a bit more environmentally aware.” ﻿ Statistics cited by Green Network Asia indicate that over 200 million pairs of flip-flops are discarded each year globally, contributing significantly to plastic and rubber pollution in landfills and oceans. Materials ‘Everywhere, Anywhere’ Eugene’s craft draws attention to the environmental impact of discarded footwear and the need for better ways to manage waste. “I source my material through landfills, the streets, literally everywhere, anywhere,” he added. (Photo: ChannelsTV/Kenny Akinwunmi) The artist shares the detailed process of how he brings each work of art to life. “My process entails getting the materials first, after which we wash them. After we wash them, we have to select and separate them according to their colours, tones, and values.” “I work in two different ways. There’s the assemblage part, where I assemble the footwear. And there’s also the tapestry, where I have to break them into tiny circles and fix them together using copper and aluminium wire,” Eugene explained. The decision is part of MSCI’s November 2026 Index Review , posted shortly after 5 p.m. ET. Official additions and deletions lists show Strategy (MSTR) out of its USA Index, which also takes it out of the broader MSCI World and ACWI indexes. The same review deletes Japan’s Metaplanet from the MSCI Japan Small Cap Index and uranium holder Yellow Cake from the MSCI United Kingdom Small Cap Index, and it removes Iceland’s Skel Fjárfestingafélag from the MSCI Iceland Frontier Markets Small Cap Index and micro-cap Upexi from the USA Micro Cap Index. All five had already been marked Deleted on MSCI’s potential-impact list , built on Sept. 30 financial data and Oct. 9 market values. Strategy is the only large-cap name in the group and, on that October list, accounted for more than 90% of the five companies’ combined float-adjusted market value. The company held 850,364 bitcoin as of Nov. 8, acquired at an average price of $75,456 a coin, or $64.16 billion in aggregate. Strategy shares closed at $122.35, up 1.06%, then slipped 1.51% to $120.50 in after-hours trading as of 5:34 p.m. ET. How the MSCI screen works The rule does not mention bitcoin. The index first checks whether a company’s operating assets equal at least 50% of total assets. Issuers that fail that core screen face five financial ratios, and a company flagged on four or more of them is ineligible for the MSCI Global Investable Market Indexes. Buffers limit turnover. A company outside the indexes cannot be added if it fails the ineligibility screen in either of its two most recent annual filing periods, but a current constituent is removed only if it fails in each of them. The index said it may also use the most recent interim filing. MSCI also said Wednesday that the same non-operating treatment will apply to the MSCI US Index Series. The screen replaces an approach aimed squarely at crypto. The index first proposed in late 2025 to exclude companies whose digital assets made up 50% or more of total assets, then dropped that plan in January and opened a broader consultation in August. It adopted the new methodology on Oct. 15, with minor modifications, and said it would end the interim measures it had placed on those companies in October 2025, including a freeze on share-count increases and a deferral of additions. entertainment.description: Two people engaging with technology in a contemporary hotel lobby work setting. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing how people learn, work, communicate and solve problems. In today’s world, if you’re not on board with AI, it could be said you’re being resistant to the fastest-growing technological innovation in the world. From students researching academic subjects to professionals developing business ideas, AI tools have become companions in everyday activities for people. They can help save time, explore new ideas, understand difficult concepts and approach tasks differently. However, as more people embrace these AI tools, it is important to understand that using AI effectively goes beyond knowing what prompts to enter. It requires knowing when to use it, how to question its responses and, most importantly, when to rely on your own knowledge and judgement. AI could make us better at what we do, not make us dependent on it. Here are ways we think you use AI effectively: Use AI as a Research Assistant One of the most effective ways to use AI is for research and information gathering. Whether you are writing an article, preparing a presentation or exploring an unfamiliar subject, AI can help you identify relevant topics, explain complex ideas and suggest areas worth investigating. You can ask it to break down unfamiliar concepts, identify key questions, or suggest research directions. However, do not treat every response as fact. Verify important information using credible sources, published research, books and reliable websites. AI can help you find information, but you are responsible for establishing what is true. Use AI to Brainstorm and Explore Ideas Like knowledge gathering, AI can brainstorm ideas with you. Sometimes, the hardest part of starting a project is knowing where to begin. AI can help you overcome this challenge by suggesting ideas, exploring different approaches and presenting perspectives you may not have considered. For writers, entrepreneurs, researchers and creatives, it can be a useful brainstorming partner. sports.title: Warriors star Steph Curry claps back at weird podcast criticism of wife Ayesha Curry
sports.description: Golden State Warriors guard Stephen Curry looks on during warmups ahead of a game on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in San Francisco. (Heather Diehl/Associated Press) HOUSTON - Stephen Curry was evidently none too pleased with social-media chatter around wife Ayesha Curry's first feature-film leading role in the romantic comedy "Second Chance Holiday." A clip from the film, featuring Ayesha Curry giving an on-screen kiss to co-star Matthew Daddario, went viral this past week and served as fodder for a wide variety of podcasts. Former NBA All-Star Gilbert Arenas and former Golden State Warriors backup Nick Young held a 17-minute segment Saturday on the kiss, with Arenas saying "the only blemish in the (Curry) family is the wife." Media personality Emmanuel Acho also devoted a good bit of airtime to the topic. On Wednesday, Curry took to Instagram for a notably pointed response. "I've been hearing a lot of noise, and usually the noise doesn't bother me, doesn't bother Ayesha, but this one in particular - when you're trying to step on the accomplishments of my wife, and obviously needing podcast tapings and topics and giving opinions on somebody else's wife - Nick, (Gilbert), Emmanuel, and anybody else who feels the need to want to have to jump in and give an opinion on something you don't really know about and kinda speaks to a bigger conversation on how you view women in this world and what they're allowed and what they're not allowed to do, even the ignorance behind how acting works," Curry said, cycling through an array of mocking faces. "Obviously, I tried to laugh this one off," he continued. "But something needs to be said. And anytime Ayesha Curry shows up in your headline, I kindly suggest you just give the happy hands, the congratulations, and maybe, just maybe, the apology can be as loud as y'all leading y'all shows with this topic." The video was clearly filmed handheld, at the spur of the moment. A source with direct knowledge of Curry's thinking said that the video response wasn't planned or organized by his team in any way, and came directly from Curry. The majority of Arenas and Young's content centered on the odd idea of Ayesha Curry potentially bringing a negative perception to the Curry family due to her acting career, visibility and independent personal success, a narrative that has existed on social media for years as her husband has simultaneously become one of the most famous athletes on the planet. Curry has increasingly dipped into the Hollywood space in recent years, starring in the animated film "GOAT" and directing the short documentary "The Baddest Speechwriter of All" this year. Back on the court, Curry has led the Warriors to an 8-3 start in 2026-27, averaging 30.6 points, 4.1 rebounds and 4.3 assists in one of the hottest early-season stretches of his career. sports.title: Princeton's Kam Mercer officially signs with UC Bearcats basketball
sports.description: Almost six months after his commitment was shown on ESPN's SportsCenter , Princeton High School senior Kameron "Kam" Mercer returned to the same room to officially sign with the Cincinnati Bearcats on Nov. 11. It was no surprise, as Mercer has been at UC games and was one of new coach Jerrod Calhoun's priorities when he arrived in town in late March. Mercer helped the Vikings win the Ohio Division I state title on March 22, then Calhoun was introduced as UC's head coach the following day. Mercer had been offered by previous coach Wes Miller's staff in eighth grade. Not long after his introductory press conference, Calhoun was on the phone with Princeton coach Bryan Wyant, asking if his staff had a chance with Mercer. The sales pitch succeeded and Mercer has been "all-in" on UC and Calhoun. After UC's difficult 63-61 loss to Minnesota, Mercer posted on X: "In him I trust" with a picture of himself with Calhoun. During his signing ceremony, he became emotional while talking about his parents, Craig and Nicole Mercer. His mother came to the podium to comfort her 6-foot-5 son. "I believe so much in Calhoun and what he's done," Mercer said. "I know he took a tough loss to Minnesota. I'm not really worried about one game. I'm super excited to get to the next level and play for him. I'm a guy that's going to come in on Day One and be a leader. Somebody that wants to win. I want to become a winner I want to become an NCAA champion." In him I trust🫡. https://t.co/jzYQJqQ4oX — Kameron Mercer (@kameron_mercer) November 10, 2026 Mercer led the Princeton Vikings to a state crown as a sophomore, averaging 14.2 points and 5.4 rebounds per game with 3.4 assists and 2.4 steals per contest. Playing at Huntington Expression Prep in West Virginia as a freshman against older talent, he averaged 11 points, 6 rebounds and 5 assists. He moved up a year scholastically to join the Bearcats for 2027-28. He also attended future teammate Josh Tyson's commitment to UC in September . Tyson played against Mercer at Lakota West but is now playing at La Lumiere in Indiana. Princeton coach Bryan Wyant has been at numerous UC basketball practices and has incorporated some of their strategies into his Vikings. Players are getting paid. Schools are navigating revenue-sharing agreements. Athletic departments are searching for new revenue streams. And lawmakers are attempting to regulate an ever-changing industry. Now, the University of Tennessee men’s basketball team is offering another possible piece of the puzzle. Tennessee players, working with Athletes.org, released a proposed collective bargaining term sheet Tuesday after months of discussions with the school’s athletic department. The exercise wasn’t intended to create a binding agreement. Instead, it was designed to show what a formal relationship between college athletes and their schools could look like. The men’s team elected Tyler Lundblade, Campbell Duncan and DeWayne Brown II to work with the college players’ union on the proposal. Negotiations stretched across August and September before both sides finalized terms on October 1. The proposal could offer a glimpse into where college athletics is headed, particularly as Congress considers new legislation and schools like Utah continue exploring different financial models. It addresses everything from player compensation and health care to transfer rules and offseason commitments. Among its more notable provisions are a salary cap and spending floor, guaranteed compensation for injured players, postseason bonuses, additional medical coverage and mutually agreed-upon transfer portal rules. It would also replace the current patchwork of revenue-sharing payments and university-affiliated NIL deals with a universal athletic services agreement that compensates athletes for playing their sports rather than completing promotional obligations. In other words, it attempts to create something college athletics has largely avoided: a more structured system in which players have a direct voice in determining the rules. The proposal isn’t a signed agreement, and Tennessee’s administration hasn’t ratified the terms. technology.title: US bit barn boom sees energy needs grow 10x as fast as grid capacity
technology.description: Datacenter power consumption in the US is growing roughly ten times faster than grid capacity, meaning facilities may soon need to find a large chunk of their own electricity from other sources. Surging demand for AI infrastructure is driving a wave of new server farms across America, but it is exposing long-term underinvestment in the grid networks required to deliver power where it's needed. Insurance broker Howden calculates that datacenters would need to source up to 58 percent of their power off the grid by 2030 just to keep their share of grid capacity from growing. Gartner warned in June that the energy consumed by AI datacenters is on track to grow 26 percent this year, and grid supply may be unable to keep pace with demand by the end of this decade. Howden's analysis of data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) and S&P Global found that since the year 2000, power being fed to data campuses has risen 19 percent a year on average, while the electricity grid expanded capacity by just 2 percent per annum over the same period. Datacenters' share of US grid capacity was circa five percent in 2025, up from 0.1 percent in 2000 – a 50-fold increase. Management consultancy Bain & Company issued a report two years ago warning that energy companies must switch gear and invest in building out grid capacity faster , as energy draw by server farms is expected to more than double by 2030. This doesn't mean that datacenters are in danger of eating all of America's electricity, at least not in the immediate future. The graph makes it appear that the two lines are about to cross, but the chart uses different scales: 1,400 gigawatts on the left axis for grid capacity, versus just 80 on the right for datacenters. Keeping datacenters at five percent of grid capacity requires 110 gigawatts of behind-the-meter capacity by 2030, Howden estimates – an expansion it considers unlikely. Instead, it expects a combination of greater reliance on the grid, slower development at power-constrained sites, and alternative supplies. For the largest, most power-constrained projects, Howden warns that grid delays of two to six years could mean $800 million to $2.4 billion in forgone revenue. "Power availability is becoming one of the defining challenges of the datacenter boom," says Howden head of Natural Resources Stuart Adam. "As demand for AI infrastructure accelerates, developers are increasingly looking beyond traditional grid connections to secure the electricity they need." Howden's business is insurance, and so Adam also notes that on-site generation introduces new operational and financial exposures, as operators take greater responsibility for their power infrastructure. ®

science.description: null A long-term goal at NASA has been the ability to robotically haul back to Earth specimens from the Red Planet. NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for its troubled Mars Sample Return (MSR) program, called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture, or PSRA in space shorthand. The plan is to establish a fresh NASA strategy for gathering Mars samples collected by the Perseverance rover and launching them back to Earth. The PSRA initiative was noted on Nov. 9 by Tiffany Morgan, director of the NASA Mars Exploration Program (MEP), during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG). Here's the PSRA strategy: Develop impartial recommendations for retrieving the Martian samples collected by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover and deliver them to Earth Assess proposed mission requirements Review prior lessons learned Evaluate current capabilities and acquisition options Morgan noted that there will be a PSRA strategy team kickoff in January 2027 with a final report due in winter 2027-2028. Pick-me-ups The backdrop to the PSRA activity is that there's one busy rover already on the Red Planet snagging and bagging samples. NASA's Perseverance Mars rover remains on the prowl within Jezero Crater following its touchdown in February 2021. That car-sized robot has been grabbing select specimens from across the area and gingerly dropping the sealed pick-me-ups on the surface of Mars , as well as stuffing them inside the rover itself. Those collectibles may well hold signs of past life on the enigmatic, dusty and foreboding Red Planet. NASA and the European Space Agency have for years been intently plotting out plans to send future spacecraft to Mars and haul those Perseverance-plucked bits, pieces, and sniffs of atmosphere to Earth for rigorous inspection here on Earth using state-of-the-art equipment. science.description:
Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston. 

Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound. Fast radio bursts, or FRBs , are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star. Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space. Catching one takes luck, as a telescope has to be pointed at the right patch of sky at the right moment. That changed with CHIME (the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) in British Columbia. With a very wide field of view and a supercomputer to process its data, CHIME more than quadrupled the number of known FRBs in its first year of operation alone. Between 2018 and 2023, CHIME recorded 4,539 bursts from 3,641 sources. As pulses of radio waves, our eyes haven't evolved to see FRBs, nor can we hear them as they aren't sound waves. Well, not until now. "Artist and composer Andrew Melchior turned all of the CHIME bursts into sound for "The Logos," an installation that has played daily at Oulu Cathedral in Finland since early April and is scheduled to run through the end of the year. Melchior and Kiyoshi Masui, an associate professor of physics at MIT, "sonified" the bursts, translating data into acoustics so that human ears can hear them. The structure of each real signal is mapped to varying musical pitches and played through 12 loudspeakers spread throughout the cathedral. The result is a range of tones, with distant FRBs humming, rumbling, popping, and whistling. The signals are old by any human measure. According to a description on Melchior's website , the youngest in the work are about 50 million years old, and the oldest are about 8 to 9 billion years old. Each burst arrives with its high frequencies first and sweeps downward, stretched by its journey through intergalactic gas, "and you can hear that dispersion as it falls from the dome," Melchior told Space.com by email. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 11, 1966: NASA launches Gemini 12 mission with astronaut icons Buzz Aldrin and Jim Lovell aboard
science.description: null On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon. Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program. It had two astronauts on board: Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin . NASA wanted to send humans to the moon. But first, it needed to make sure crews had the right skills, like docking vehicles in space and taking spacewalks. Before Gemini 12, astronauts struggled with spacewalks because there weren't enough handholds on their spacecraft. NASA made some spacewalk changes for Gemini 12. Aldrin performed three spacewalks and spent more than five hours working in space with no major problems. Gemini 12 also successfully docked to an unpiloted Agena booster that launched the same day. The astronauts returned to Earth after four days in space. Both Aldrin and Lovell went on to join the Apollo program . Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon during Apollo 11 , and Lovell became the commander of Apollo 13 . The Gemini 12 astronauts James Lovell and Edwin Aldrin lifted off aboard a Titan launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center on November 11, 1966, an hour and a half after their Agena target vehicle was orbited by an Atlas rocket. (Image credit: NASA/MSFC) Why it mattered Gemini 12 may have closed out NASA's Gemini program of two-person space missions, but it established the mission also established the fundamentals of spacewalking that Apollo astronauts would use when they walked on the moon. It's fitting that Aldrin was the primary spacewalker of the mission. A rookie astronaut (and the first to earn a Ph.D.), Aldrin set a precedent by training for his spacewalk in a neutral buoyancy pool in Maryland to better simulate working in weightlessness. Then he did it again as the second person to walk on the moon on Apollo 11. "This approach became so successful, underwater training has become the primary spacewalk training method used by the United State, Russia and China," NASA officials said in a mission overview . "Today, NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston is large enough to include mockups of major sections of the International Space Station . As such, it is the largest indoor body of water in the world, with 6.2 million gallons of water." science.title: Blood-thinning drug limits cartilage damage and relieves osteoarthritis pain
science.description: Coloured X-ray of osteoarthritis of the knee ALAIN POL/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY A drug that prevents blood clots reduced pain and improved mobility in mice and monkeys with knee osteoarthritis. The approach seems to partly work by reducing inflammatory signals that degrade cartilage. Osteoarthritis is caused by the wear and tear of cartilage that cushions the ends of bones, leading to inflammation, pain and stiffness. It affects more than 500 million people worldwide. Painkillers and anti-inflammatory drugs can relieve symptoms, but no approved drugs halt or slow worsening of the disease. “We have nothing to offer our patients apart from suggesting weight loss, or offering drugs that provide pain relief,” says Tonia Vincent at the University of Oxford, who wasn’t involved in the study. Advertisement Read more The best non-drug therapies to relieve the pain of knee osteoarthritis It is widely thought that inflammatory molecules called TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta drive inflammation that worsens osteoarthritis. This has led to clinical trials testing drugs that target either of these molecules. But these have been unsuccessful, potentially because these molecules compensate for each other when one is blocked, according to Chuan-Ju Liu at Yale University and his colleagues. To explore whether targeting both molecules may be more effective, the researchers surgically removed part of the cartilage in the left knee joints of eight monkeys to mimic wear and tear that triggers osteoarthritis. science.title: Andy Weir's 'Exoplanet' just landed on Audible, but what actually makes an exoplanet habitable?
science.description: null Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead. This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo . Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable? Learning from the stars An artist's concept illustrates a young, red dwarf star surrounded by three planets. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock. For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it. Using a technique called spectroscopy , astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance. Astronomers use these measurements to determine whether a world lies in the habitable zone of a star, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on the surface given a suitable atmosphere. A planet orbiting a cool red dwarf would need to be much closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun to be in this habitable zone. Unfortunately, being in this zone is no guarantee of a planetary paradise. Hostile stars Black holes are bad news for life, but living stars provide just as many problems. (Image credit: Audible) A planet that sits comfortably in the habitable zone is ultimately still at the mercy of its star. Stars emit more than just the light we see. Ultraviolet radiation and X-rays can interact with planetary atmospheres, altering chemistry and even contributing to the loss of the atmosphere . Violent stellar flares can produce bursts of high-energy radiation. A planet could offer a wonderfully balmy temperature, only to be bombarded with radiation from the host star. science.title: Who will step up to preserve space age artefacts for future generations?
science.description: NASA/JPL-Caltech Around 40,000 years from now, the Voyager 1 probe will pass within astronomical spitting distance of the star Gliese 445. From there, it will continue drifting through the universe on an endless journey that marks humanity’s first attempt to reach the stars. Voyager 1 – which on 18 November will have travelled one light day from Earth – began its odyssey almost 50 years ago, meaning it has been operating for the majority of the space age. That makes it a rarity: most of our iconic spacecraft ended their lives burned up in Earth’s atmosphere or in bits at the bottom of the ocean. Two of the most important missions still flying today, the Hubble Space Telescope and the International Space Station, look set to share the same fate in the near future, even as scientists call for Hubble to be preserved . While some craft like the space shuttles are on display in museums, our present space history is, essentially, in its dark ages, with little thought currently given to preserving spacecraft in situ, where our space-travelling descendants may wish to marvel at them. Even the Apollo hardware left behind on the moon has almost no protection in international law. Advertisement Perhaps we need an organisation like the UNESCO World Heritage Committee to designate important space artefacts for preservation, and encourage funding from cultural and heritage budgets, not scientific ones, to do this. Of course, with such budgets often under threat and the US set to leave UNESCO at the end of this year, this could introduce new problems. Private philanthropy is another option. If humanity is to one day take its place among the stars, a fantasy that fuels many a tech billionaire, it would be a great shame to not be able to look back at how we got there. Just as we remember 19th-century captains of industry like Andrew Carnegie and J. P. Morgan for funding great cultural institutions, perhaps we should be lobbying for the creation of a Musk Space Museum or Bezos Orbital Institute.

Shot by Roger Patterson and Robert Gimlin in 1967, the clip became one of the canonical pieces of evidence for the existence of Bigfoot: a mythical humanoid that supposedly lives in the forests of North America. Bigfoot is one of the icons of cryptozoology, the search for probably-nonexistent creatures. It has hordes of devotees. In Capturing Bigfoot , film-maker Marq Evans uncovers what really happened in 1967. He speaks to Patterson’s associate Bob Heironimus, who says he wore an ape costume in the footage. Crucially, Evans also finds a lost piece of 16-millimetre film, shot in 1966, showing a rehearsal for the final Patterson-Gimlin video. science.title: Did comets bring building blocks of life to Earth? Scientists aren't so sure anymore
science.description: The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet. Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth . Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space? New research led by planetary scientist Richard Anslow of the Institute for Astronomy at the University of Cambridge has now seemingly ruled out comets as the origin of complex organic molecules on Earth. "Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said Anslow in a statement . Stripping the romance from the Earth's turbulent past Comet impacts on Earth were much more frequent in the first half-billion years of the solar system ’s existence, when there were still lots of debris leftover from the formation of the planets. For over a century comet impacts had been considered a prime suspect in the search for what brought the building blocks of life to Earth. However, while comets bringing the building blocks of life to Earth is "kind of a romantic idea," according to Anslow, the University of Cambridge researcher added that the team's results suggest that is highly unlikely. Anslow and colleagues arrived at this conclusion based upon computer modeling by using the very latest simulations depicting the origin and evolution of comets and their orbits, their interactions with Earth's atmosphere as they enter it, and of the hypervelocity comet impacts themselves. In particular, they used the fate of hydrogen cyanide as a proxy for what happens to complex organic molecules in comet impacts. Hydrogen cyanide is frequently found in comets and was even detected in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS . An artist’s impression of a comet crashing into the early Earth (Image credit: Scarlett White) The problem is that comets are generally moving at too great a velocity. For organic molecules to survive impact, the impact velocity would have to be below 33,500 miles per hour (15 kilometers per second). Anslow and his colleagues found that, in general, comets travel too fast and enter Earth’s atmosphere at too sharp an angle for complex organic molecules to survive. Instead, they are mostly vaporized on impact. Even on the rare occasions that the complex organic molecules survived, they were usually not in great enough abundance to provide any meaningful prebiotic chemistry. science.title: 'There's tremendous demand': Rocket Lab raises price of Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million
science.description: null The coming launch bottleneck has ramped up demand for a rocket that has yet to leave the ground. Rocket Lab announced on Monday (Nov. 9) that it recently raised the price of a Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million — an increase of more than 25%, for a ride on a rocket that's set to debut in 2027. "Launch is extremely constrained, and that is exactly the situation we predicted," Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said on Monday during the company's third-quarter earnings call. "We saw a pent-up launch market on the horizon, and rather than provide early discounted launches, we set out to deliver a rocket into an environment with extreme demand at full price or higher." Rocket Lab is best known for Electron , a workhorse small-satellite launcher that debuted in 2017 and now has 90 orbital missions under its belt. The 59-foot-tall (18 meters) expendable rocket and can haul 660 pounds (300 kilograms) to low Earth orbit (LEO). Neutron is the company's entry into the medium-lift market. It features a reusable first stage, stands 141 feet (43 m) tall and can carry 14.3 tons (13 metric tons) of payload to LEO. Rocket Lab announced Neutron back in 2021 and first targeted a 2024 debut for the vehicle. But various problems have cropped up over the years, pushing things back. Last month, for example, Rocket Lab announced that it was delaying the first Neutron flight from late 2026 into 2027 due to a manufacturing issue (which it says is now under control). Such setbacks have not dampened demand for Neutron's services, however. During Monday's call, Beck revealed that Rocket Lab booked eight Neutron launches during the third quarter of 2026, which ran from July 1 through Sept. 30. The contracts for those eight flights are worth "a total of roughly 515 million, including multiple missions on a new escalated base price of $70 million," Beck said. Neutron's first 16 launches are now sold out, he added, and bookings from here on will be for flights in the 2030s. "The demand is a function of both a tightening global launch supply and our customers' confidence that Rocket Lab is the right partner to break the world's launch bottleneck," Beck said. science.title: Hubble Space Telescope reveals glittering stars with mysterious origins | Space photo of the day for Nov. 11, 2026
science.description: null The Hubble Space Telescope has captured a breathtaking view of thousands of stars glittering like cosmic jewels in a dazzling display of blue, gold and orange. But this spectacular scene is far more than just a pretty picture. Some of these stars are almost as old as the universe itself and could hold clues to how our Milky Way formed. M30 is a globular star cluster located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth. (Image credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini) What is it? The exquisite image released by ESA on Nov. 5 shows Messier 30 (M30), a densely packed collection of stars located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth in the constellation Capricornus. M30 is a globular cluster, a roughly spherical collection of tens of thousands to millions of stars held together by gravity . Our Milky Way is home to at least 150 of these ancient stellar gatherings, some of which are estimated to be between 11.5 billion and 13.5 billion years old. For comparison, the universe itself is approximately 13.8 billion years old! Why is it amazing Besides looking like a vast cosmic treasure trove glittering across the universe, M30 also has a fascinating story to tell. Globular clusters are essentially cosmic time capsules. Their ancient stars preserve chemical clues about the conditions that existed when they formed, helping astronomers piece together the Milky Way's early history. Astronomers have also discovered that M30, along with several other globular clusters, traverses the Milky Way in the opposite direction to the galaxy's rotation. This unusual motion raises the intriguing possibility that M30 may not have formed in our galaxy at all. It could have simply been captured by the Milky Way billions of years ago.

science.title: NASA's new UVEX space telescope will peer deep into the universe's most violent events
science.description: null A new NASA space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility. The Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX) mission, developed by NASA in conjunction with the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), will be the first mission to create deep all-sky maps in ultraviolet light. Thus, when it launches in 2031, UVEX will join new sky-mapping surveys like NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer), which scans the cosmos in infrared, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which does the same over the southern hemisphere in visible light, in creating deep-sky maps across a broad swathe of the electromagnetic spectrum. UVEX's ultraviolet views will reveal explosive events such as the collisions between ultra-dense stellar corpses called neutron stars and the supernova explosions that mark the deaths of massive stars and the births of neutron stars and black holes. Additionally, the NASA ultraviolet telescope should be able to detect a multitude of low-mass galaxies much closer to the Milky Way than similar galaxies that are currently being observed millions and even billions of light-years away by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) . The $590 million UVEX mission will "advance fundamental frontiers in astrophysics, from understanding the smallest galaxies to diagnosing the aftermath of neutron-star mergers and other cosmic explosions," the mission's principal investigator, Caltech physics professor Fiona Harrison, said in an Oct. 27 statement . "The first major ultraviolet space mission in two decades, UVEX is a bold leap forward in our exploration of the ultraviolet universe," Caltech President Ray Jayawardhana said in the same statement. UVEX will paint a picture of cosmic life, death and afterlife UVEX will benefit from a major leap forward in UV sensitivity thanks to its Caltech-built sensors, which are based on complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) imaging technology. This will help the spacecraft tap into what Harrison described as "the untapped opportunity in the UV." UVEX will be uniquely poised to spot millions of nearby, small, and faint galaxies that are teeming with infant stars that emit bright UV light. "In optical light, it's very hard to distinguish these nearby galaxies from faraway ones that look similar," Harrison said. "UV light will make them easier to find." UVEX won't just be investigating the infancy of stars , however. It will also examine the deaths of ancient stars in the form of supernovas. NGC 4449: Small Galaxy, Big Impact Explanation: Don’t judge a galaxy by its size. Our home galaxy, the Milky Way , is about 100,000 light years across. This huge expanse of space contains hundreds of billions of stars! The smallest galaxies, called dwarf galaxies , are about 1/10th the size of the Milky Way and only contain a few billion stars. They are also the most common type of galaxy in the whole universe. Today’s image shows one such dwarf galaxy, NGC 4449 , captured by the Hubble Space Telescope . NGC 4449 and similar dwarf galaxies are missing more oxygen than models predict. The storms alleviated short-term drought conditions in the Southwest but caused river levels to spike to record or near-record levels in places, triggering damaging floods. One effect of the heavy rains detected by satellites was the rapid rise of water levels in Navajo Reservoir. The change is visible in the images above, acquired on September 20 (left) and November 7 (right) with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 . In that time, the lake in northern New Mexico and southern Colorado rose by nearly 60 feet (18 meters), according to data from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. (Note that the Bureau of Reclamation decreased releases from Navajo Dam on September 16 and 17.) On November 7, the reservoir stood at its highest level since August 2019 and at 108 percent of the average capacity for that date. That contrasts with September 20, when it held just 60 percent of its average capacity. Due to snow drought across the West in winter 2025-26, the lake saw relatively little growth in the spring, when snowmelt often raises water levels. The San Juan, Piedra, and other rivers swelled with runoff amid the wet weather. Pagosa Springs, Colorado, a town along the San Juan River about 40 miles (64 kilometers) northeast of the lake, was especially hard-hit by flooding. In the first round of rain, 5.05 inches (12.8 centimeters) fell in the town, and on October 23 the river reached major flood stage . After more rain, the river spiked again on November 1, this time nearly to the record level set in 1911 during a devastating flood . Officials issued evacuation orders, and responders rescued dozens of people, according to news reports , while water inundated streets and damaged property. Heavy rain and flooding have been widespread across southwest Colorado, southeast Utah, northern Arizona, and northwest New Mexico in recent weeks.
